title: Lay out cutting templates on streaky glass: with the streaks, along one edge
instruction: Lay the three white templates flat on the amber glass sheet, ready to trace. Turn each one so its long side runs along the sheet's streaks. Keep every template at least 8 mm in from the sheet's edges and at least 5 mm from the others, and line them up along one long edge of the sheet so that a strip at least 8 cm wide stays clear along the other long edge. Then let go and move the grippers at least 3 cm away from the templates.
context: Before cutting, a stained-glass maker lays the pattern templates on the sheet and checks the layout. Each template's grain arrow must run parallel to the glass's streaks, or the texture runs the wrong way in the finished panel. Pieces stay clear of the sheet's rough rolled edge and a few millimetres apart, leaving room for the cutter wheel and the break. They are lined up from one edge so the rest of the sheet stays one usable strip; cutting pieces from the middle of a sheet wastes it. The check is a top photo and a steel rule: edge allowances, gaps, the width of the clear strip, and arrows parallel to the streaks. Done by stained-glass artists, leaded-glass glaziers and studio glass cutters (O*NET 27-1012.00 craft artists, 47-2121.00 glaziers). Expensive art glass makes layout and yield a real cost. The turn comes from the streaks, which run across the sheet's outline, and where the group sits decides the yield.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Four things are on the table, nothing else. (1) Glass sheet: a stand-in for a sheet of streaky amber cathedral glass, rigid, 180 mm along x by 300 mm along y and 3 mm thick, taped down so it cannot move, centred at x 29.0 cm, y 0. Its near long edge is at x 20.0 cm, its far long edge at x 38.0 cm, its short ends at y -15.0 cm and +15.0 cm. It is made of 12 straight strips side by side along y, each 180 x 25 x 3 mm and running the sheet's full 180 mm along x, alternately dark amber (sRGB 0.62, 0.32, 0.06; the strip at y -15.0 to -12.5 cm is dark) and light amber (sRGB 0.96, 0.76, 0.38). So the streaks run front to back, along x, across the sheet's short side. Its top is flat, 3 mm above the table. (2) Template A1: a white acrylic block standing in for a paper pattern template, 70 x 40 x 12 mm, 40 g, lying flat on the table centred at x 20.0 cm, y +36.0 cm, its 70 mm long side along y: it spans x 18.0 to 22.0 cm and y 32.5 to 39.5 cm. (3) Template A2: the same block (70 x 40 x 12 mm, 40 g, white acrylic), lying flat centred at x 32.0 cm, y +36.0 cm, its long side along x: it spans x 28.5 to 35.5 cm and y 34.0 to 38.0 cm. (4) Template B: a white acrylic block, 60 x 40 x 12 mm, 34 g, lying flat centred at x 26.0 cm, y -36.0 cm, its 60 mm long side turned 45 degrees from x, its far end toward -y (its long side points forward and to the right). On every template the grain arrow runs along its long side; in simulation the arrow is not drawn and the long side stands for it. Both large faces of a template are alike, so either may face up. One friction coefficient (the simulator's default) for everything.
scoring: The score is read from the state on the last step. A template is LAID when all of these hold: (a) flat: tilted less than 3 degrees; (b) directly on the glass: its lowest point within 2 mm of the sheet's top and its centre over the sheet (a template lying on another is 12 mm too high); (c) at rest: its centre moved along a path of less than 2 mm over the last 0.5 s; (d) let go: both grippers' fingers at least 30 mm from the template, judged on a round zone about each gripper's axis, from its finger tips 38 mm up and as wide as its fingers reach at any heading (60 mm from the axis when fully open), so an open finger resting on a template counts as touching it; (e) every corner of its outline seen from above at least 8 mm inside every edge of the sheet; (f) at least 5 mm, seen from above, from every other template lying low (its lowest point within 20 mm of the sheet's top: one lying on another counts, one carried higher does not); (g) its long side within 5 degrees of the streaks (the x axis), either way round. CLEAR STRIP, once all three are laid: the larger of the distance from the near long edge (x 20.0 cm) to the nearest template corner and from the far long edge (x 38.0 cm) to the nearest template corner. Score 1.0 if all three templates are laid and the clear strip is at least 80 mm (exactly 80 mm counts). Otherwise 0.2 for each laid template: 0.6 for three (for example spread across the middle, or in two rows), 0.4 for two, 0.2 for one, 0 for none. A template earns nothing if it is turned more than 5 degrees off the streaks, less than 8 mm from a sheet edge, tilted, moving, lying on another template, still held, has a gripper's fingers less than 30 mm from it, or is off the sheet (on the table or the floor). This costs the others nothing except by the gap rule: a template less than 5 mm from another lying low loses its credit, and so does the other one (so one lying on another also voids the one under it). Success is the 1.0 condition: held for 1 s it ends the trial; otherwise the trial runs to its limit and the same rule is read on the last step. Doing nothing scores 0 (every template starts on the table). Possible scores: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0. Nominal end state (1.0): one row along y near the near long edge, long sides along x, centres at x 25.4 cm and y +6.0 cm (A1), 0 (A2) and -6.0 cm (B); gaps 20 mm, 19 mm (A) and 24 mm (B) in from the near edge, 70 mm from each short end, clear strip 91 mm. For 1.0 every template's x span must lie within x 20.8 to 30.0 cm (or 28.0 to 37.2 cm along the far edge). Real trial, with the grippers open and away, from a top photo with a steel rule and a protractor: each template's nearest point to each sheet edge (at least 8 mm), the gaps between templates (at least 5 mm), each long side's angle to the streaks (5 degrees or less), the clear strip from the far (or near) edge to the nearest template (at least 80 mm), and every finger at least 30 mm from every template (a 30 mm gauge block), with each gripper's fingers swept round its axis to every heading, as the simulation judges; a template that rocks or does not lie flat on the glass is not laid.
fidelity: The sheet is fixed and rigid; its streaks are straight 25 mm coloured strips (real streaks are irregular and finer). Real templates are paper, card or thin plastic; 12 mm white acrylic blocks stand in so a top-down gripper can hold them by their ends. They are rectangles (border pieces), so face up or face down does not matter. No tracing or cutting is simulated: the task is the layout before tracing.
reset_notes: Put the templates back at their start positions and turns: A1 centred at x 20.0 cm, y +36.0 cm, long side along y; A2 at x 32.0 cm, y +36.0 cm, long side along x; B at x 26.0 cm, y -36.0 cm, long side at 45 degrees with its far end toward -y. Nothing is consumed. For real trials, seam (sand) the glass sheet's edges and tape it down, or use a striped acrylic sheet of the same size.
